div.head: SUBSECT. 9.
Of the Rational Soul.
div.p:
In the precedent Subsections I have anatomized those inferior faculties of the soul; the Rational remaineth, a pleasant, but a doubtful subject (as Velcurio.one terms it), and with the like brevity to be discussed. Many erroneous opinions are about the essence and original of it; whether it be fire, as Zeno held; harmony, as Aristoxenus; number as Xenocrates; whether it be organical, or inorganical; seated in the brain, heart or blood; mortal or immortal; how it comes into the body. Some hold that it is ex traduce [by traduction], as Phil. 1 de Anima, Tertullian, Lactantius de opific. Dei cap. 19, Hugo lib. de Spiritu & Anima, Vincentius Bellovic. spec. natural. lib. 23 cap. 2 & 11, Hippocrates, Avicenna, and many Goclenius in Ψυχολ. pag. 302, Bright in Phys. Scrib. lib. 1, David Crusius, Melanchthon, Hippius, Heurnius, Levinus Lemnius, &c.late writers; that one man begets another, body and soul: or as a candle from a
candle, to be produced from the seed: otherwise, say they, a man begets but half a man, and is worse than a beast that begets both matter and form; and besides the three faculties of the soul must be together infused, which is most absurd as they hold, because in beasts they are begot, the two inferior I mean, and may not be well separated in men. Lib. an mores sequantur, &c.Galen supposeth the soul crasin esse, to be the Temperature itself; Trismegistus, Musaeus, Orpheus, Homer, Pindarus, Pherecydes Syrius, Epictetus, with the Chaldees and Egyptians, affirmed the soul to be immortal, as did those Briton Caesar. 6 Com.Druids of old. The Read Aeneas Gazaeus’ dial. of the immortality of the Soul.Pythagoreans defend Metempsychosis, and Palingenesia, that souls go from one body to another, epota prius Lethes unda [having first swallowed down the water of Lethe], as men into Wolves, Bears, Dogs, Hogs, as they were inclined in their lives, or participated in conditions.

lg.l: Possumus ire domus, pecudumque in corpora condi.
[… We can make our homes inside wild beasts,
And be lodged in the flesh of cattle.]

div.p: In Gallo.Lucian’s Cock was first Euphorbus a Captain:

lg.l: Ovid. met. 15.Ille ego (nam memini) Trojani tempore belli,
[I myself (for I remember), at the time of the Trojan War,

div.p: a horse, a man, a sponge. Nicephorus hist. lib. 10 cap. 35.Julian the Apostate thought Alexander’s soul was descended into his body: Plato in Timaeo, and in his Phaedon (for aught I can perceive) differs not much from this opinion, that it was from God at first, and knew all, but being enclosed in the body, it forgets, and learns anew, which he calls reminiscentia, or recalling, and that it was put into the body for a punishment, and thence it goes into a beast’s, or man’s, as appears by his pleasant fiction de sortitione animarum [about the allotting of souls], lib. 10 de rep., and after Phaedro.10,000 years is to return into the former body again,

lg.l: ——— Claudian lib. 1 de rap. Proserp.post varios annos, per mille figuras,
Rursus ad humanae fertur primordia vitae.
[… after many years, through a thousand forms,
He attains again the beginning of human life.]

div.p: Others deny the immortality of it, which Pomponatius of Padua decided out of Aristotle not long since, Plinius Avunculus cap. 7. lib. 2 & lib. 7 cap. 55, Seneca lib. 7 epist. ad Lucilium epist. 55, Dicaearchus in Tull. Tusc., Epicurus, Aratus, Hippocrates, Galen, Lucretius lib. 1,

lg.l: [Besides, we perceive that the mind is born with the body,
Grows together with it, and ages as it does]

div.p: Averroes, and I know not how many Neoterics. This question of the immortality of the Soul, is diversely and wonderfully impugned and disputed, especially amongst the Italians of late, saith Jac. Colerus lib. de immort. animae, cap. 1. The Popes themselves have doubted of it, Leo Decimus that Epicurean Pope, as Colerus ibid.some record of him, caused this question to be discussed pro and con before him, and concluded at last, as a profane and atheistical Moderator, with that verse of Cornelius Gallus,

lg.l: Et redit in nihilum, quod fuit ante nihil.

div.p: It began of nothing, and in nothing it ends. Zeno and his Stoics, as De eccles. dog. cap. 16.Austin quotes him, supposed the Soul so long to continue, till the Body was fully putrefied, and resolved into materia prima [primordial matter]: but after that, in fumos evanescere [to disappear in smoke], to be extinguished and vanish; and in the meantime, whilst the body was consuming, it wandered all abroad, & e longinquo multa annunciare [to relate many things from a distance], and (as that Clazomenian Hermotimus averred) saw pretty visions, and suffered I know not what.

lg.l: Ovid. 4 Met.Errant exangues sine corpore & ossibus umbrae.
[The bloodless shades wander without body or bones.]

div.p:
Others grant the immortality thereof, but they make many fabulous fictions in the meantime of it, after the departure from the body: like Plato’s Elysian fields, and that Turkey Paradise. The souls of good men they deified; the bad (saith Austin) became devils, as they supposed; with many such absurd tenets, which he hath confuted. Jerome, Austin, and other Fathers of the church, hold that the Soul is immortal, created of nothing, and so infused into the child or Embryo in his mother’s womb, six months after the Some say at 3 days, some 6 weeks, others otherwise.conception; not as those of brutes, which are ex traduce, and dying with them, vanish into nothing. To whose divine treatises, and to the Scriptures themselves, I rejourn all such Atheistical spirits, as Tully did Atticus, doubting of this point, to Plato’s Phaedon. Or if they desire Philosophical proofs and demonstrations, I refer them to Niphus’, Nic. Faventinus’ tracts of this subject. To Fran. and John Picus in digress. sup. 3 de Anima, Tholosanus, Eugubinus, To. Soto, Canus, Thomas, Peresius, Dandinus,
Colerus, to that elaborate tract in Zanchius, to Tolet’s 60 reasons, and Lessius’ 22 arguments, to prove the immortality of the soul. Campanella lib. de sensu rerum, is large in the same discourse, Albertinus the Schoolman, Jacob. Naclantus, Tom. 2. op., handleth it in four questions, Anthony Brunus, Aonius Palearius, Marinus Mersennus, with many others. This Reasonable Soul, which Austin calls a spiritual substance moving itself, is defined by Philosophers to be the first substantial act of a Natural, Human, Organical Body, by which a man lives, perceives, and understands, freely doing all things, and with election. Out of which definition we may gather, that this Rational Soul includes the powers, and performs the duties of the two other, which are contained in it, and all three faculties make one Soul, which is inorganical of itself, although it be in all parts, and incorporeal, using their Organs, and working by them. It is divided into two chief parts, differing in office only, not in essence. The understanding, which is the Rational power apprehending; the will, which is the Rational power moving: to which two, all the other Rational powers are subject and reduced.
